framework.name: STAR / PAR
framework.one_liner: Takes a completed event apart into the Situation the actor faced, the Task they owned, the Actions they took and the Result those actions produced, so that agency and causal attribution have to be stated rather than implied.

slots.label: Situation
slots.description: The context before anything was done: who was involved, where, what had just happened and what was at stake. Normally stated, because narrators open with it.

slots.label: Task
slots.description: The objective or responsibility the actor owned in that situation: what had to be achieved, by when, and why it mattered. Often implied by the situation and the actions rather than said.

slots.label: Action
slots.description: What the actor actually did, as concrete first-person steps in order; the slot that exposes agency ('I' rather than 'we').

slots.label: Result
slots.description: What happened afterwards, measured where possible, and to which action it is attributed. The outcome is usually stated; the attribution often is not.

slots.label: Problem (PAR)
slots.description: PAR variant: Situation and Task collapsed into a single statement of the problem the actor faced. Used here as a derived compression of the stated situation and task.

relations.label: sets up
relations.description: situation gives rise to the task

relations.label: causes
relations.description: generic causal attribution between any two nodes

examples.title: Clearing a support backlog before renewals (interview answer)
examples.summary: Which action produced which result is the one thing this textbook STAR answer never says. A support lead narrates a billing incident, the brief she was given, three concrete actions and the measured outcome; the graph separates what she states from what an interviewer has to infer.

source.title: Interview answer: tell me about a time you delivered under pressure
source.text: In my second year as support team lead at a mid-sized software company, we shipped a billing update in March that double-charged about four hundred customers. Within two days, complaints about the charge had pushed the ticket queue from a normal sixty open tickets to over nine hundred, and our average first response time went from four hours to three days. Two of my six agents were on leave that month. I was asked to get the queue back under control before the quarterly renewals in April. First, I wrote a one-page macro that explained the bug and the refund timeline, and I had it sent proactively to all four hundred affected accounts before they wrote in; new tickets fell by half the next day. Second, I split the queue so that the two most experienced agents took only refund cases and the rest handled everything else. Third, I asked finance to process the refunds in one batch instead of case by case. By the end of the third week the queue was back under eighty tickets and the first response time was under five hours. Our renewal rate in April was 94 percent, one point higher than the previous quarter. Afterwards we made the proactive notice a standard step for any billing incident.
source.attribution: Written for this library as a behavioural-interview answer, the setting in which STAR was popularised (DDI's Targeted Selection); the company and figures are invented.

nodes.label: Billing update double-charged ~400
nodes.text: A billing update shipped in March double-charged about four hundred customers.
nodes.source_quote: we shipped a billing update in March that double-charged about four hundred customers

nodes.label: Queue: 60 to over 900 in two days
nodes.text: Within two days, complaints about the charge pushed the open-ticket queue from a normal sixty to over nine hundred.
nodes.source_quote: complaints about the charge had pushed the ticket queue from a normal sixty open tickets to over nine hundred

nodes.label: First response: 4 hours to 3 days
nodes.text: Average first response time went from four hours to three days.
nodes.source_quote: our average first response time went from four hours to three days

nodes.label: Two of six agents on leave
nodes.text: Two of the six support agents were on leave that month.
nodes.source_quote: Two of my six agents were on leave that month

nodes.label: Demand 15x, capacity two-thirds
nodes.text: Ticket volume rose roughly fifteen-fold while the team ran at two-thirds of its normal capacity.
nodes.rationale: Arithmetic on stated figures (900 against 60 tickets, four of six agents); the speaker never states the ratio, but it is what makes the situation critical rather than merely busy.

nodes.label: Control the queue before renewals
nodes.text: The lead was asked to get the queue back under control before the quarterly renewals in April.
nodes.source_quote: I was asked to get the queue back under control before the quarterly renewals in April

nodes.label: Real objective: protect renewals
nodes.text: The underlying objective was to protect April renewal revenue from the affected customers, not merely to shrink the queue.
nodes.rationale: The deadline is tied to renewals and the speaker reports the renewal rate as a result; the text never states retention as the goal, only the queue.

nodes.label: Incident, short staff, renewals
nodes.text: PAR compression: a self-inflicted billing incident flooded a short-staffed support team a few weeks before quarterly renewals.
nodes.rationale: PAR collapses Situation and Task into one problem statement; choosing which facts constitute the problem (the incident, the staffing gap, the renewal deadline) is the analyst's framing, not the speaker's words. 0.80 is the 0.70-0.85 band of the shared confidence scale and means: not that this compression is the only possible one, but that most careful readers given these sentences would draw the problem boundary here.

nodes.label: Macro sent proactively to 400 accounts
nodes.text: Wrote a one-page macro explaining the bug and the refund timeline and had it sent proactively to all four hundred affected accounts before they wrote in.
nodes.source_quote: I wrote a one-page macro that explained the bug and the refund timeline, and I had it sent proactively to all four hundred affected accounts before they wrote in

nodes.label: Split queue: experts take refunds
nodes.text: Split the queue so that the two most experienced agents took only refund cases and the rest handled everything else.
nodes.source_quote: I split the queue so that the two most experienced agents took only refund cases and the rest handled everything else

nodes.label: Asked finance to batch refunds
nodes.text: Asked finance to process the refunds in one batch instead of case by case.
nodes.source_quote: I asked finance to process the refunds in one batch instead of case by case

nodes.label: New tickets halved next day
nodes.text: New tickets fell by half the day after the proactive notice went out.
nodes.source_quote: new tickets fell by half the next day

nodes.label: Queue under 80 by week three
nodes.text: By the end of the third week the queue was back under eighty tickets.
nodes.source_quote: By the end of the third week the queue was back under eighty tickets

nodes.label: First response under five hours
nodes.text: By the end of the third week the first response time was under five hours.
nodes.source_quote: the first response time was under five hours

nodes.label: April renewals 94%, up one point
nodes.text: The renewal rate in April was 94 percent, one point higher than the previous quarter.
nodes.source_quote: Our renewal rate in April was 94 percent, one point higher than the previous quarter

nodes.label: Proactive notice made standard
nodes.text: The proactive notice became a standard step for any billing incident.
nodes.source_quote: we made the proactive notice a standard step for any billing incident

nodes.label: Uplift attributable to response?
nodes.text: The part of the April renewal uplift that the incident response produced, if any; the attribution is the speaker's implication, not a stated measurement.
nodes.rationale: The speaker places the renewal figure after the actions, inviting the listener to credit them, but gives no base rate or comparison; a one-point move could be normal quarter-to-quarter noise. Kept below 0.50 because STAR requires every Result to be attributed to an Action, so the slot has to be filled even where the answer leaves the attribution speculative.

edges.source_quote: complaints about the charge had pushed the ticket queue
I was asked to get the queue back under control
First, I wrote a one-page macro
Third, I asked finance to process the refunds
before they wrote in; new tickets fell by half the next day
Afterwards we made the proactive notice a standard step

edges.rationale: 'Back under control' names the queue; the response-time collapse is the same problem seen from the customer's side, but the speaker does not name it as part of the brief.
With a third of the team out, splitting the queue reads as a response to the staffing gap; the speaker never connects the two.
The computed gap between demand and capacity is what 'back under control' had to close.
The proactive notice reaches every affected account before renewal; it serves retention, not only queue size.
PAR reading: the problem statement, not the brief, is what the first action answers.
Halving inbound is the largest lever on the backlog; the text credits no single action with the week-three figure.
Specialising the experienced agents on refund cases plausibly cut handling time; the speaker lists the action without attributing the response-time result to it.
A single refund batch closes the refund tickets together; no result is attributed to it in the text.

Of the three actions, the proactive notice is the one most plausibly felt by renewing customers. Kept below 0.50 because the framework requires the Result slot to be attributed to an Action; the low figure marks the attribution as the speaker's implication, not a stated link.
The renewal figure is the only fact r5 can rest on; kept below 0.50, matching r5, because the framework requires the attribution slot filled.

examples.title: Windsurf's wild weekend: selling the company Google left behind
examples.summary: Speaker-stated attribution sits here beside attribution only an analyst can supply. Three days after Google DeepMind hired away Windsurf's founders, the interim CEO Jeff Wang and Cognition's CEO Scott Wu tell how the remaining company was sold over a weekend: what they faced, what Wang set out to do, what each of them did hour by hour, and what the team got.

source.episode_title: Windsurf's Wild Weekend, SpaceX Invests $2B into xAI, Zuck's AI Data Supercluster (Jeff Huber, Scott Wu, Jeff Wang, Carl Pei, Garrett McCurrach)

examples.why_this_episode: A completed 72-hour event narrated by the two people who did it, three days after it happened. The Situation is on the record (founders and engineers hired by Google DeepMind, a commercial team left behind and being poached, hundreds of angry employees), Wang states his Task in so many words ('my immediate priority was...'), the Actions are timed (24 hours of calls, a next-day meeting with a paper agreement, signing two hours before the announcement) and the Results are measurable and read from the announcement (100% participation, cliffs waived, accelerated vesting) then confirmed on air (standing ovation, product and GTM team intact). Some causal links are stated by the speakers and some are not, which is exactly the distinction STAR exists to force.

nodes.label: Founders, engineers hired by DeepMind
nodes.text: Google DeepMind hired Windsurf's founders Varun Mohan and Douglas Chen and part of its engineering team, in a deal that left the rest of the company behind.
nodes.source_quote: very excited to welcome Windsurf AI founders, Mohan and Douglas Chen, and some of the brilliant Windsurf engineering team to Google DeepMind
nodes.source_ref: host reading Demis Hassabis's post, L78-L84

nodes.label: Left behind: sales, enterprise, GTM
nodes.text: What remained at Windsurf after the founders left was the commercial organisation: sales, enterprise, account management and go-to-market.
nodes.source_quote: the people that got left behind at Windsurf were sales, enterprise, account management, GTM

nodes.label: Hundreds of angry employees
nodes.text: Jeff Wang was now running a company of hundreds of employees who were angry about what had just happened.
nodes.source_quote: you now run a company with hundreds of employees that are angry about what just happened

nodes.label: A tough Friday; nobody wanted his shoes
nodes.text: Wang calls the Friday of the founders' departure a tough one; nobody would have wanted to be in his position.
nodes.source_quote: It was a tough it was a tough Friday, I'll say. I don't think anybody would want to be in my shoes on Friday.

nodes.label: 'Just a shell' vs code, product, team
nodes.text: Outsiders said what was left was just a shell; Cognition looked and saw the code, the product, the customers and, most importantly, the whole team.
nodes.source_quote: people were saying, well, the thing that's left is just a shell. And we looked at it and we said, well, actually, I don't know if that's right. There's the code, there's the product, there's the customers, and most importantly, there's the whole team

nodes.label: Cognition over-focused on engineers
nodes.text: Scott Wu says Cognition tends to over-focus on software engineers because that is who they are and how they think.
nodes.source_quote: we tend to over-focus on software engineers because it's just who we are and how we think about it

nodes.label: Windsurf had built out all functions
nodes.text: Windsurf's team had built out sales, deployed engineering, enterprise work, infrastructure, marketing, operations and finance.
nodes.source_quote: the whole team have built out a really great kind of suite of all the different kinds different functions, right? Sales, deployed engineering, enterprise work, infrastructure, marketing, operations, and so on, finance, et cetera.

nodes.label: Teams circling the GTM team
nodes.text: Over the weekend other companies were circling, wanting to hire away Windsurf's go-to-market team.
nodes.source_quote: over the weekend, I'd heard other teams that were kind of circling, wanting to hoover up their GTM team

nodes.label: Priority: many options, paths forward
nodes.text: Wang's immediate priority was to get many options on the table and have many paths forward, and to give the team a path immediately because it was happening now.
nodes.source_quote: My immediate priority was just to get a lot of options on the table and to have a lot of paths forward. I had to tell the team like, this is the path forward immediately because this is happening now.

nodes.label: Keep team, customers from scattering
nodes.text: The objective behind the options was to find a home for the whole company before the sales and go-to-market staff accepted the offers circling them.
nodes.rationale: Follows from the stated facts that other teams were trying to hire away the GTM team and that hundreds of employees were angry; Wang states his priority as options and paths, never as retention.
nodes.idea: The gap this weekend exposed is a market on two sides: research-heavy AI labs that over-index on engineers can buy a built-out commercial organisation whole instead of growing one, and the employees a founder-only hire strands have no default protection until an acquirer improvises it.

nodes.label: No founders, poachers, no time
nodes.text: PAR framing: a funded company with product, customers and a commercial team but no founders, an angry staff and competitors poaching, with days rather than weeks to find an answer.
nodes.rationale: Collapses the stated situation and Wang's stated priority into one problem statement; which facts count as the problem and the time bound are the analyst's framing. 0.80 is the 0.70-0.85 band of the shared confidence scale: most careful readers given these quotes would draw the same boundary, though 'days rather than weeks' is read from the sequence and stated by nobody.

nodes.label: Talked to many AI companies
nodes.text: Windsurf talked to a lot of teams, among them many AI and foundation-model companies. Wang says 'we talked', without saying who made which call.
nodes.source_quote: we talked to a lot of teams out there. There's a lot of AI companies, foundational companies.

nodes.label: 24 hours on the phone after all-hands
nodes.text: After the all-hands, Wang was on the phone for roughly 24 hours nonstop.
nodes.source_quote: I was on the phone for pretty much 24 hours, nonstop on my phone after the all hands

nodes.label: Met Scott next day; paper agreement
nodes.text: Wang and Wu worked fast: they met at Windsurf's office the next day and Wu brought the agreement on paper to sign.
nodes.source_quote: me and Scott, we worked really fast. We met at our office the next day. He even brought in everything on a piece of paper to sign.

nodes.label: Signed 1-2 hours before announcing
nodes.text: The documents were signed one or two hours before the announcement went out. The speaker says 'we got things signed', without naming the signatories.
nodes.source_quote: we got things signed like one or two hours before we were able to put out the announcement

nodes.label: Chose Cognition: 'done in my mind'
nodes.text: After talking to Scott Wu and the Cognition team the decision was made; Wang adds that Cognition was the only other team they thought was smarter than their own.
nodes.source_quote: after talking to Scott and the Cognition team, it was done in my mind. There's a done deal. I don't know if you guys know this, but Cognition was probably the only other team that we thought was smarter than our team, actually.

nodes.label: Made the deal deliberately generous
nodes.text: Wang, Wu and the team went out of their way to make the acquisition very generous to employees.
nodes.source_quote: So me and Scott and the team, we really went out of our way to make this a very generous acquisition

nodes.label: Acquired by Cognition
nodes.text: Windsurf is being acquired by Cognition in what Wang calls a real acquisition.
nodes.source_quote: this is a this is a real acquisition. Okay, we are being acquired by cognition

nodes.label: 100% participate; cliffs waived
nodes.text: All Windsurf employees participate financially, vesting cliffs are waived and, per the same announcement, vesting is fully accelerated.
nodes.source_quote: 100% of windsurf employees will participate financially they will also have all their vesting cliffs waves what and will receive fully accelerated vesting for their work today

nodes.label: Standing ovation; sentiment shifted
nodes.text: At the Monday all-hands the team cheered with something like a standing ovation; the sentiment has shifted and the team is more fired up.
nodes.source_quote: They kind of cheered for like a standing ovation or something. So I think the sentiment has shifted. The team is even more fired up to go.

nodes.label: Product and GTM intact, plus Devin
nodes.text: The whole product and the GTM team are still there, and the team now also has Devin to sell.
nodes.source_quote: The whole product is still there. All the things we had and the GTM team is still there. And now they also have Devon to sell as well.

nodes.label: Deal done in a couple of days
nodes.text: The deal was done in just a couple of days.
nodes.source_quote: the fact that they were able to get this deal done in just a couple of days is fantastic

nodes.label: Speed kept the GTM team from leaving
nodes.text: Closing within days is what preserved the go-to-market team as an asset; a slower process would have lost people to the teams circling them.
nodes.rationale: Combines three stated facts (competitors circling, a couple-of-days close, the team still there); the counterfactual that a slow process would have lost them is nobody's statement.

edges.source_quote: this is the path forward immediately because this is happening now

edges.rationale: The connective is the host's question ('you were all of a sudden managing a team of hundreds of people that probably all wanted your time and attention'), not Wang's answer; the link from the angry team to his stated priority is a reading across two speakers, which the question makes natural but nobody states.

edges.source_quote: My immediate priority was just to get a lot of options on the table
What is the best use of my time? I can tell you I was on the phone for pretty much 24 hours
after talking to Scott and the Cognition team, it was done in my mind. There's a done deal.
we got things signed like one or two hours before we were able to put out the announcement
So me and Scott and the team, we really went out of our way to make this a very generous acquisition

edges.rationale: Wang says 'me and Scott, we worked really fast'; the host, in a different segment, says the deal was done in just a couple of days. The two facts are barely contestable together, but no single turn joins them, so the edge is derived rather than fact.

Both facts are the host's and adjacent, but joined only by 'And': that the commercial team left behind is the team the other companies were circling for is co-reference ('their GTM team') the reader completes, not a stated cause.

edges.source_quote: All the things we had and the GTM team is still there. And now they also have Devon to sell as well

edges.rationale: Narrative order only: the priority statement answers the Friday, but Wang never links the two explicitly.
Sequence: the decision precedes the next-day meeting; Wang does not say the meeting was arranged because of it.

The paper agreement brought to the meeting is what got signed; stated as sequence, not as cause. The edge also carries a4's agency: 'we got things signed' names no signatories, and reading them as the two who met over the paper agreement in a3 is the analyst's attribution.
Competitors poaching the GTM team is what makes keeping the company whole the real objective.
A 24-hour phone marathon makes sense as a race against attrition; Wang gives no reason for the pace.
Generous terms are a retention device; Wang presents the generosity without stating its purpose.
Wang juxtaposes the generous terms with the ovation ('so I think the sentiment has shifted'); the causal claim is implied, not stated.
The speed of the close is the premise of the inferred preservation of the team.
If speed prevented departures, the intact GTM team is its consequence.
A buyer existed because Cognition valued what outsiders called a shell; nobody states this as the reason the deal happened.
PAR reading: the compressed problem, not the stated priority, is what the search for buyers answers.

Agency claim for a1: Wang says 'we talked to a lot of teams' but, in the same answer, 'I was on the phone for pretty much 24 hours'; reading the phone marathon as the act behind the plural 'we' credits him with the outreach. He never says who else called.

Wu's admission that Cognition over-focuses on software engineers is, together with s7, the complementarity reading of why a commercial organisation was worth buying rather than redundant. Wu declines the causal claim himself: 'I wouldn't say it was intentional.'

The suite of functions Windsurf had built out is the other half of that complement, and what there was left to buy once the founders and part of engineering had gone. Wu presents the fit as a coincidence, not a motive.
Grounds the idea t2 carries rather than its text: the buyer's engineer skew is one half of the market reading.
Grounds the idea: the built-out commercial functions are what a lab short of them could buy whole.
Grounds the second half of the idea: the protections had to be written into this deal because nothing makes them a default.
